analysis.one_liner: Seeds private investment accounts for newborns that would then pay their Social Security benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and then its Social Security subcommittee, where it died with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a personal investment account for every person born after mid-1999, seeded with $1,000 of federal money. Account holders could invest in a handful of funds run much like the retirement plan for federal employees, and could add up to $7,000 a year, deducting $2,000 of it from their taxes. When they retire, their monthly Social Security checks would be paid first out of their own account, with anything past the balance coming from the traditional system. The seed money would be financed by reducing the share of taxes on retirement benefits that goes to Medicare's Hospital Insurance fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Every child born after mid-1999 would start life with a $1,000 government-seeded account. Anyone could contribute up to $7,000 a year and deduct $2,000 whether or not they itemize, a tax break that is worth most to people with spare cash to save. Insurers and professional asset managers would gain: the law would require the government to buy an annuity contract from a private insurer for each retiring account holder, and fixed-income funds would be run by 'qualified professional asset managers.'
analysis.who_benefits_short: Newborns, contributing savers, insurers and fund managers

how_it_helps.text: Each eligible individual born on or after July 1, 1999 would receive a $1,000 initial government contribution to a personal investment account established automatically at birth.

Account holders could choose among investment options modeled on the Thrift Savings Plan for federal employees, including a government securities fund, a fixed income fund, and a stock index fund, with government securities as the default for anyone who does not choose.

Individuals could contribute up to $7,000 per year to their account and take an above-the-line income tax deduction of up to $2,000 per year, available even to taxpayers who do not itemize deductions.

The bill includes spousal protections: a married account holder defaults into a joint-and-survivor annuity unless the couple jointly waives it, and account balances would be subject to court orders for child support, alimony, and judgments for child abuse.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare's Hospital Insurance trust fund would lose revenue: the bill finances the initial $1,000 contributions by reducing that fund's appropriations of taxes on retirement benefits. Account holders who choose the stock or fixed income funds would bear the market risk themselves; the bill requires them to sign an acknowledgment that the government does not protect against loss or guarantee a return. The Treasury would also forgo revenue from the new $2,000-per-year tax deduction.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare's trust fund, account holders, and the Treasury

drawbacks.text: Account holders electing the fixed income or stock funds must sign an acknowledgment that the investment is at their own risk, that the government does not protect them against loss, and that no return is guaranteed.

Under the bill, monthly Social Security benefit payments to account holders would be paid first out of their own account balance, with the traditional system paying only amounts beyond that balance — so the account largely prefunds benefits the holder would receive anyway rather than adding money on top, and a poorly performing account gets consumed faster.

The financing mechanism reduces appropriations to the Medicare Hospital Insurance trust fund of taxes on retirement benefits to pay for the initial contributions, shifting money from one promised benefit to another.
The $2,000 annual tax deduction is worth the most to households that already have cash to save; families with no spare income get only the one-time $1,000 seed.
Every retiring account holder's balance would be used to purchase an annuity from a private insurer, routing the payout through insurance companies rather than direct government payment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes a real give with a real take. A $1,000 birth stake and a $2,000-a-year deduction give ordinary families a head start on savings. But the fine print makes the account a prefunding vehicle: it pays the holder's own Social Security benefits first, so it substitutes market performance for part of the traditional guarantee rather than adding to it, and the required risk acknowledgment is honest about that. Taking the seed money out of Medicare's Hospital Insurance fund trades one promised benefit against another. On balance, the people best served would be those with money to contribute and the financial firms selling the annuities and managing the assets.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House subcommittee until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Petri introduced the bill on June 17, 1998, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Six days later, on June 23, 1998, it was referred to the subcommittee on Social Security.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, Medicare's Hospital Insurance trust fund kept the retirement-benefit tax revenue the bill would have redirected, and the traditional Social Security benefit structure was left untouched. Insurers and asset managers lost the prospect of a new stream of mandated annuity and asset-management business.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare's trust fund and traditional Social Security

for.name: Rep. Thomas E. Petri
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral; never scheduled a markup or sent the bill to the floor.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Social Security
against.role: Subcommittee that received the referral on June 23, 1998
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no member of either party cosponsored, so the record shows no support or opposition from either party beyond the sponsor himself.

industries.note: The bill requires the government to purchase an annuity contract from a private insurer for each retiring account holder, creating a guaranteed customer stream. Insurer margins on those contracts would come out of account holders' retirement balances.
Fixed-income investment funds would be run by 'qualified professional asset managers,' and administrative expenses would be paid out of the trust fund's net earnings, reducing account returns.

industries.industry: Medicare Hospital Insurance program (and its beneficiaries)
industries.note: The bill pays for the $1,000 birth stakes by reducing that fund's appropriations of taxes on retirement benefits, draining money from Medicare to seed the new accounts.

industries.industry: Higher-income households with savings to invest
industries.note: The $2,000 annual above-the-line deduction and up to $7,000 in annual contributions favor people who already have spare cash; the tax preference is financed by all taxpayers.
